query: For a CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix evaluated in sliding from room temperature to 800 °C, what single intervention could overcome the difficulty of maintaining low coefficient of friction and wear rate throughout the full temperature range? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains the mechanism expected to operate across the test regime, predicts performance relative to the starting CoCrFeNi material, specifies relevant temperature, load, and environmental boundaries, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes a controlled falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a small amount of reactive alloying elements (such as Ti, Nb or V) into the CoCrFeNi matrix will trigger in situ formation of a nanohierarchical heterostructure that releases frictional stresses via multiple deformation pathways at room temperature and, importantly, promotes rapid formation of a protective nanocrystalline glaze layer during high‐temperature sliding. This cooperative microstructural mechanism should yield a lower and more stable coefficient of friction and reduced wear rates over the entire temperature range.
generation.material_initial_state: A conventional, single-phase CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy with a homogeneous microstructure.
generation.intervention: Microalloying the CoCrFeNi base with a controlled, low concentration of reactive elements (e.g., Ti, Nb, V) designed to form in situ nanoprecipitates and induce a nanohierarchical heterostructure.
generation.conditions: Sliding wear tests conducted over a temperature range from room temperature to 800 °C, under a normal load around 5 N and typical sliding speeds in an ambient or controlled environment where tribo‐oxidation can occur.
generation.structural_mediator: The in-situ formed nanohierarchical structure, comprising nano-coupled grains and dispersed nanoprecipitates, which at low temperatures facilitates multiple adaptive deformation pathways and at high temperatures accelerates the development of a dense, nanocrystalline glaze layer.
generation.mechanism: At room temperature, the enhanced heterogeneous microstructure distributes and relaxes frictional stresses by activating various deformation mechanisms, thereby lowering the friction coefficient. At elevated temperatures, increased tribo-oxidation interacts with the adaptive nanostructure to form a protective glaze layer that reduces adhesive and oxidative wear.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the unmodified CoCrFeNi alloy, the modified alloy is expected to exhibit a significantly lower and more stable coefficient of friction and a markedly reduced wear rate from room temperature up to 800 °C.
generation.baseline: The original single-phase CoCrFeNi alloy, which typically suffers higher friction and severe wear at high temperatures due to surface softening, adhesive wear, and insufficient tribochemical protection.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is expected to hold for sliding conditions with normal loads around 5 N, sliding speeds similar to those in referenced studies, and within the temperature interval from approximately 25 °C to 800 °C; performance under significantly different mechanical stresses or environments remains to be verified.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal type and concentration of added reactive elements are not precisely known, nor is the long-term thermal and mechanical stability of the nanohierarchical structure under cyclic or extreme operating conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one being the baseline CoCrFeNi alloy and the other being the alloy microalloyed with a low concentration of reactive elements (e.g., Ti, Nb, or V). Subject both sets to identical sliding wear tests over the temperature range from room temperature to 800 °C under a constant load (≈5 N) and comparable sliding speed. Use real-time monitoring of the coefficient of friction and post-test wear analysis.
measurements: Real-time coefficient of friction across the temperature range
Wear volume and specific wear rate calculations post-test
Surface and cross-sectional microstructural analysis (e.g., SEM, EDS) to detect the formation of nanoprecipitates and the protective glaze layer
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the microalloyed samples do not show a statistically significant reduction in friction coefficient and wear rate (or do not form a distinct adaptive nanostructural glaze) compared to the baseline CoCrFeNi alloy across the tested temperature range, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractSustained wear damages on the sliding surfaces of alloys are generally the culprit responsible for the failure of various mechanical systems. Inspired by high-entropy effects, here we deliberately deploy nanohierarchical architecture with composition undulation in a Ni50(AlNbTiV)50 complex concentrated alloy, which yields ultralow wear rate within the order of 10−7 to 10−6 mm3/Nm between room temperature and 800 °C. Such remarkable wear resistance heretofore represents one of the highest wear resistance reported for the bulk alloys or composites, and originates from the multi-type adaptive friction interface protection governed by intrinsically nano-coupled grains and nanoprecipitates. This cooperative heterostructure releases gradient frictional stress in stages upon wear at room temperature through the coexistence of multiple deformation pathways while activating a dense nanocrystalline glaze layer upon wear at 800 °C to minimize adhesive and oxidative wear. Our work uncovers a practical avenue for tailoring wear properties with multicomponent heterostructures over a wide temperature range.

AbstractA novel metal matrix composite CrMnFeCoNi with Y2O3 as reinforcement phase was designed and manufactured by mechanical alloying and spark plasma sintering. After sintering at 900 °C for 5 min, the microstructure consisted of a FCC matrix and Y2O3 nanoparticles. The addition of 0.25 wt % Y2O3 increased the room temperature tensile strength of the CrMnFeCoNi base from 868 MPa to 1001 MPa, while the mechanical properties of the addition of 0.5 wt % Y2O3 composite decreased. In the meantime, the addition of Y2O3 had no significant influence on the coefficient of friction, while the addition of 0.25 wt % Y2O3 composite shows excellent wear-resistance.Keywords: high-entropy alloys, mechanical alloying, metal-matrix composites, Y2O3 nanoparticles, mechanical properties, tribological properties
